newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss speed Holocaust fund, public money unsettled.
newsitem.headline: Swiss speed Holocaust fund, public money unsettled.

text.p: The Swiss government agreed on Wednesday to create immediately a memorial fund that taps contributions from banks and other businesses to aid victims of the Holocaust, Foreign Minister Flavio Cotti said.

But he rebuffed calls for a quick cabinet decision on what payment Switzerland itself would make, insisting Berne had to await the first findings of a historians' panel examining Switzerland's wartime role as a financial centre.

"As an immediate first step, a special fund will be opened," drawing on contributions from the private sector to offer quick assistance to Hitler's victims and their needy relatives, no matter what their faith or race, Cotti said.

Galvanised by international pressure, the country's three bigest banks last week agreed to put up 100 million Swiss francs ($70 million) as a humanitarian gesture to aid Holocaust victims and their families. Other businesses pledged to follow suit.

Berne is coordinating the fund, which aims to assure Jewish groups and other critics that the Swiss are taking seriously allegations they cynically profited from World War Two and that banks hoarded the dormant wealth of Holocaust victims.
But Cotti made clear Berne was not about to be badgered into a quick financial commitment of taxpayers' money for the fund, as some business executives and politicians have suggested.
"The decision on whether the government will take part financially will be based on comprehensive, solid facts," he declared.

The panel's first findings on Swiss purchases of looted gold from Nazi Germany and Switzerland's anti-Jewish wartime immigration policy that turned back 30,000 refugees -- most of them Jews -- as the Holocaust raged are due within months.

"When the reports are available, the cabinet will make decisions very quickly," Cotti said, adding Berne was considering setting up a foundation before summer whose role would be broader than the first fund.
He hailed private businesses' willingness to pay into a humanitarian fund and said the Federal Council, or cabinet, was ready to take the political lead in administering the programme.

"But let's not forget: banks and businesses can do what they want with their money. The Federal Council has to answer to the taxpayer," he said. "I am convinced the Swiss people will have understanding for this way of proceeding."

He hinted that Berne was trying to groom public opinion to support such a payment and avoid a damaging referendum drive amid opinion polls that show half the Swiss would just as soon assign the past to history books.
"It takes some time, but only if we base our actions on facts and create the conditions for a broad discussion will we be in position to draw the appropriate conclusions," he said.
"Such decisions can only be made with broad popular support, especially under (the Swiss system of) direct democracy."
Swiss Jewish leaders hailed the move.

"It is certainly good that a structure is being created quickly for a special fund with these 100 million Swiss francs from the banks, so that the money doesn't just sit there," said Thomas Lyssy, vice president of the Swiss Jewish Federation (SIG).
"It is also important that the Federal Council is preparing a definitive structure. A foundation is just what the SIG has already proposed."
He said it was "reasonable" for Berne to await the historical findings before deciding on a contribution because it would take that long to agree on the final fund structure.
